HARDWARE EXPLAINED

Read the spec sheet. Then read between the numbers.

Payload, runtime, degrees of freedom: what the headline figures leave unanswered.

H
HUMANOID EditorialResearch, hardware & practical perspectives
EDITORIAL DATE5 Oct 20262 min read

Manufacturer imagery used for editorial illustration. A product image does not imply affiliation or a hands-on review.

IN THIS STORY
01Ask what the payload means02Give runtime a workload03Treat degrees of freedom as a design description04Keep an evidence column→Your next stepExplore hardware ↗
THE KEY IDEA

A specification becomes useful when you know its configuration, test conditions, and relevance to your task.

Specifications compress a complex machine into a few numbers. That is useful for discovery, but it can hide the conditions behind the measurement. The goal is not to collect the highest values. It is to understand which figures describe the operating conditions you actually expect.

01

Ask what the payload means

Check whether the stated payload is per arm or total, whether it is sustained or momentary, and where the object is held. Reach and posture can change what a useful handling task looks like. Ask the manufacturer to demonstrate the exact combination of object, motion, and duration you require.

02

Give runtime a workload

Standing, walking, manipulating, and running onboard computation are different operating conditions. A runtime figure without a workload is difficult to use in planning. Request the test scenario, charging approach, and any battery exchange procedure. Then map those conditions onto a typical working cycle.

03

Treat degrees of freedom as a design description

A joint count describes aspects of a mechanism, not its ability to complete your application. It does not replace information about joint limits, control access, sensing, or hand design. A platform with fewer joints can still suit a specific task better if its reach and interfaces match the job.

04

Keep an evidence column

Add a source URL, configuration, and review date beside each value in your comparison sheet. Distinguish manufacturer-stated figures from your own measurements. Where conditions are absent, write a question. That habit prevents a tidy spreadsheet from becoming more certain than the underlying information.

MAKE IT PRACTICAL

Your next step.

  • Record measurement conditions.
  • Check model and hardware revision.
  • Translate each specification into a task requirement.
